questions.question: D0 — Add gstack skill routing rules to CLAUDE.md? gstack-plan-count-7Lu8Et / main branch. ELI10: gstack works best when your project's CLAUDE.md tells Claude Code which skill to invoke for common tasks (strategy → /plan-ceo-review, bugs → /investigate, etc.). Without routing rules, you have to type the skill name every time. With them, Claude Code routes automatically when the situation fits. Stakes if we pick wrong: minor — routing rules are a few lines and easy to remove. Recommendation: A because the project already uses gstack skills and routing pays off immediately. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. Pros / cons: A) Add routing rules to CLAUDE.md (Recommended): ✅ Claude Code auto-invokes the right skill based on what you're doing — no manual /skill typing needed ✅ Skills like /ship and /autoplan benefit from downstream routing when chained ❌ Adds ~20 lines to CLAUDE.md (trivially reversible). B) Skip — invoke skills manually: ✅ Zero change to CLAUDE.md — one less thing to manage ✅ Full control over which skill runs and when ❌ You type /skill-name every invocation — adds friction over time. Net: routing rules are low-cost, high-frequency savings; the only real question is whether you want Claude Code opinionated about which skill fits which task. <gstack-qid:routing-injection>

questions.question: D2 — Which implementation approach for the two new tests? Branch: main. ELI10: The plan specifies two tests. The question is how much precision to bake into the plan's assertion spec. Approach A locks down exactly the plan's stated scope. Approach B enriches that scope with concrete assertion contracts — what 'correct receipt' means field by field and what 'fails clean' means as an exception type. Approach B costs maybe 5 minutes extra with CC and prevents tests that pass against wrong behavior. Stakes if we pick wrong: A) a test that asserts 'receipt != nil' passes even if fields are wrong. B) slightly more spec to write, but pins the behavioral contract tightly. Recommendation: B because payment tests that don't assert the right fields are false confidence — an empty receipt still 'generates a receipt.' Completeness: A=7/10, B=10/10. A) Minimal viable — two tests as written (Completeness 7/10): ✅ Implements exactly what the plan says, no scope creep ✅ Leverages existing factory/mock/sleeper as-is ❌ 'Correct receipt' and 'fails clean' are underspecified — tests could pass against wrong behavior. B) Full behavioral contract — two tests + explicit assertion specs (Completeness 10/10, Recommended): ✅ Pins specific receipt fields (charge ID, amount, currency, timestamp) in the happy path ✅ Pins exception type + mock call count + backoff delay assertions in the 502 path ✅ Tests reject wrong behavior, not just non-nil results ❌ ~20-30 extra lines of spec in the plan (human: 0 extra / CC: ~2 min). Net: the difference between a test that proves correctness and a test that proves execution.

options.description: Two tests exactly as the plan specifies, using existing factory/mock/sleeper. No additional assertion spec.

questions.question: D3 — Which review mode? Branch: main / test coverage plan. ELI10: The review mode sets how aggressive I am about scope. This plan adds two unit tests and explicitly keeps production behavior unchanged. HOLD SCOPE means I make those two tests bulletproof without suggesting additional work. SELECTIVE EXPANSION means I also surface cherry-pick opportunities (additional test cases, idempotency tests, contract tests) that you can opt into. Recommendation: HOLD SCOPE because this is a test coverage fix — the scope is correct and deliberately narrow; adding cherry-picks risks scope creep on payment-critical code that should ship fast. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. A) HOLD SCOPE — make it bulletproof (Recommended): ✅ Maximum rigor on the two tests as specified ✅ No scope drift on payment-critical code ❌ Won't surface additional test opportunities (idempotency, 402 via processPayment(), concurrent charge). B) SELECTIVE EXPANSION — hold scope + cherry-picks: ✅ Same rigor PLUS individual opt-ins for additional test cases ✅ You decide each expansion ❌ Takes longer ❌ Risk of scope creep before the core two tests even ship. C) SCOPE REDUCTION — find the bare minimum: ✅ Useful if the plan is overbuilt ❌ This plan is already minimal — nothing to cut without losing the stated goals. Net: HOLD SCOPE is right for a bounded test coverage task. <gstack-qid:ceo-mode-selection>

questions.question: D4 — Section 2: 'fails clean' is undefined — what does the 502 test actually assert? Branch: main. ELI10: The plan says 'assert retry-with-backoff fires once, then fails clean.' 'Fails clean' is ambiguous. In payment code, it could mean: (A) a specific exception is raised (caller catches it explicitly — best for observability and correctness), (B) an error object is returned (acceptable, but caller must check it), or (C) the test just asserts no uncaught exception and the method returns — silent failure. If the implementer picks C, a test that 'fails clean' tells you nothing about whether the failure is visible to callers. Stakes if we pick wrong: a silent-failure contract in processPayment() means callers think payment succeeded when it didn't — the worst possible payment bug. Recommendation: A because payment failures must propagate explicitly; silent returns are dangerous in money code. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. A) Specify the exception contract (Recommended): ✅ Test asserts a named exception (e.g., PaymentExhaustedError) is raised ✅ Pins the behavioral contract callers depend on ✅ Failure is never silent ❌ Requires knowing the actual exception class name (which should already exist in the codebase). B) Specify an error return value: ✅ Explicit failure signal without exceptions ❌ Callers can forget to check the return value ❌ Payment processing code typically uses exceptions for control flow on failures. C) Leave 'fails clean' to the implementer: ✅ Zero change to plan scope ❌ Implementer may choose a silent-failure path and the test will still pass. Net: 'fails clean' in a payment path must mean 'visible failure' — specify which. <gstack-qid:ceo-502-failure-contract>

options.description: Add to plan: the 502 test asserts processPayment() returns an error/failure object (no exception).

questions.question: D5 — Section 6: should the 502 test assert the Stripe mock was called exactly twice? Branch: main. ELI10: The plan says 'an exhausted 502 operation makes exactly two charge attempts' and that the factory 'exposes the Stripe mock call history.' This is available infrastructure for an explicit assertion, but the plan doesn't say the test USES it. Without the assertion, a buggy implementation that retries 5 times (or never retries) would still 'fail clean' and the test would pass. The mock call history is already wired — asserting on it costs zero extra infrastructure. Stakes if we pick wrong: if the test skips this assertion, the retry-with-backoff behavior is untested even though the test claims to test it. Recommendation: A because 'retry fires once' is a behavioral guarantee the plan explicitly states — testing behavior without asserting the behavior is a gap. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. A) Add to plan: assert mock call count = 2 (Recommended): ✅ Proves the retry loop ran exactly once (not 0, not 5) ✅ Uses already-wired mock call history ✅ Fast to add ❌ One more assertion in the test (minimal cost). B) Skip — leave call count implicit: ✅ Plan stays minimal ❌ Retry count behavior is untested — a buggy loop is invisible to the test. Net: the mock call history is free; not using it leaves the retry behavior on faith. <gstack-qid:ceo-mock-call-count>

questions.question: D6 — Section 6: should the 502 test assert the virtual sleeper was called with an expected backoff delay? Branch: main. ELI10: The plan says the virtual sleeper 'records backoff without real delays.' The 502 test currently says 'assert retry-with-backoff fires once' — but 'fires' is ambiguous. Without a sleeper assertion, a buggy implementation that retries with no delay (or with the wrong delay) would still pass the test. The sleeper is already wired to the factory. Asserting the delay value proves the backoff is real, not just that a retry happened. Stakes if we pick wrong: without a delay assertion, a future diff could zero-out the backoff config and no test would catch it. Recommendation: A because backoff is the 'with-backoff' in retry-with-backoff — it's the contract. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. A) Add to plan: assert sleeper called with expected delay (Recommended): ✅ Proves backoff is non-zero and correct value ✅ Catches future regressions that remove delay config ✅ Sleeper already wired, zero extra setup ❌ Requires knowing the configured backoff delay value. B) Skip — leave backoff timing implicit: ✅ Plan stays minimal ❌ A future zero-backoff regression is silent ❌ 'Retry-with-backoff' is only half-tested. Net: the sleeper is wired to record the delay; not asserting on it wastes the investment. <gstack-qid:ceo-backoff-assertion>
